title: Layer codes as quantum memories: syndrome extraction, thresholds and idle robustness
abstract: Layer codes are three-dimensional local CSS codes of check weight at most six, obtained by quasi-concatenating a CSS input code with unrotated surface code patches. What is established about them describes the code, not the circuit that measures it. In this work, we evaluate them as active memories under circuit-level noise. Doing so first requires a syndrome extraction circuit, and the junction stabilizers that couple the patches rule out borrowing a surface code patch's CNOT schedule. We present a decoder-free scheduler that constrains hook propagation first and compresses depth afterwards, generate circuits for eighteen layer codes across four input codes, and compare them with surface codes of the same distance, simulated and decoded in the same way. The circuits lose no distance to hook errors on [[4,2,2]]-input codes wherever a circuit-distance proof is affordable, and reach a lower logical error rate than those of a general-purpose scheduler for CSS codes at roughly half its CNOT depth per round. Our primary family built from a [[4,2,2]] input code reaches a circuit-level threshold of $5.06(7)\times 10^{-3}$. The layer code outperforms the surface code in terms of idle robustness: at the same distance it tolerates an interval between syndrome extraction rounds 1.7-3.0 times longer than the rotated surface code. This comes at the cost of 1.7-5.0 times more operations per unit time and approximately five times more physical qubits, both per logical qubit. Finally, we model the cost of the beyond-2D cross-plane CNOTs that the construction demands, and find that their speed matters far more than their fidelity.
summary: This work analyzes layer codes as advanced quantum memories by simulating their performance under realistic circuit-level noise. The authors introduce a novel scheduling technique that improves circuit depth and achieves superior idle robustness compared to surface codes. The findings suggest layer codes are highly competitive, provided the associated hardware overheads are manageable.
main_problem: The paper evaluates layer codes as active quantum memories under realistic circuit-level noise, focusing on the complex syndrome extraction circuit required for repeated measurements.
main_result: Layer codes achieve lower logical error rates than general-purpose schedulers at half the CNOT depth per round and significantly outperform surface codes in idle robustness, though this comes with higher overhead.
method: The authors developed a novel, decoder-free scheduler that constrains hook propagation first and compresses depth afterward, comparing the resulting circuits against standard surface code implementations.
model_or_system: The system utilizes layer codes, which are 3D local CSS codes formed by quasi-concatenating a CSS input code with unrotated surface code patches, for quantum error correction.
key_observables: Logical error rate (LER), circuit depth (CNOT depth per round), idle robustness (sustainable idle interval), and physical overhead (qubits, gates per logical qubit).
important_parameters: Circuit-level noise threshold ($p_{th}$), distance ($d$), and the ratio of idle time tolerance (1.7-3.0 times longer than rotated surface code).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on active circuit-level fault-tolerance, and the cost analysis emphasizes that the speed of beyond-2D cross-plane CNOTs is more critical than their fidelity.
figures_summary: The notes reference tables comparing metrics (ticks/round, CNOTs/round) for layer codes and surface codes, and figures illustrating the code structure with input codes like [[4,2,2]].
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the challenge of syndrome extraction circuits, proposing a two-phase scheduler (constraining hook propagation, then compressing depth), and finally comparing the resulting performance metrics (LER, robustness) against established codes.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, quantitative benchmarks for next-generation QEC hardware by rigorously analyzing circuit overheads and noise resilience beyond simple code distance arguments.
